questions.text:
Let [latex]G[/latex] be a simple, finite, undirected graph with vertex set [latex] \{v_1,...,v_n\}[/latex]. Let [latex] \Delta (G)[/latex] denote the maximum degree of [latex]G[/latex] and let [latex] N=\{1,2,...\} [/latex] denote the set of all possible colors. Color the vertices of [latex]G[/latex] using the following greedy strategy: for [latex]i = 1,...,n[/latex]
[latex]color(v_i)\leftarrow min\{ j \in N: \text{ no neighbour of } v_i \text{ is colored } j\}[/latex]
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Each vertex gets the smallest colour not used by any neighbour, so no edge joins equal colours [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] proper colouring [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- A vertex has at most [latex]\Delta(G)[/latex] neighbours, so among colours [latex]1\ldots\Delta+1[/latex] one is always free [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] at most [latex]\Delta(G)+1[/latex] colours [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]K_n[/latex] needs n = [latex]\Delta+1[/latex] colours, so "at most [latex]\Delta(G)[/latex]" is FALSE.
- A bad vertex order can use more colours than the chromatic number (e.g. on some bipartite graphs) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: This procedure results in a proper vertex coloring of [latex]G[/latex].
The number of colors used is at most [latex] \Delta (G)+1[/latex].
The number of colors used is at most[latex] \Delta (G)[/latex].
The number of colors used is equal to the chromatic number of [latex]G[/latex].

questions.text:
Consider a random experiment where two fair coins are tossed. Let A be the event
that denotes HEAD on both the throws, B be the event that denotes HEAD on
the first throw, and C be the event that denotes HEAD on the second throw.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
[latex]P(A)=\frac14,\ P(B)=P(C)=\frac12[/latex].

- A and B: [latex]P(A\cap B)=P(A)=\frac14\ne P(A)P(B)=\frac18[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not independent (same for A and C).
- B and C: [latex]P(B\cap C)=\frac14=\frac12\cdot\frac12[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] independent.
- So [latex]P(B|C)=P(B)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: B and C are independent; Prob(B|C) = Prob(B)

questions.text:
Let [latex]X[/latex] be a set and [latex]2^X[/latex] denote the powerset of [latex]X[/latex].
Define a binary operation [latex] \Delta [/latex] on [latex]2^X[/latex] as follows:
[latex]A \Delta B=(A-B) \cup (B-A)[/latex]
Let [latex] H=(2^X,\Delta ) [/latex]. Which of the following statements about [latex]H[/latex] is/are correct?
questions.solution:
Check the group properties of symmetric difference on [latex]2^X[/latex]:
- Closed: [latex]A\Delta B\subseteq X[/latex]
- Associative: yes (it behaves like XOR on membership)
- Identity: [latex]\phi[/latex], since [latex]A\Delta\phi=A[/latex]
- Inverse: [latex]A\Delta A=\phi[/latex], so every A is its own inverse (not its complement: [latex]A\Delta A^c=X[/latex])

Answer: H is a group; the inverse of A is A

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Every element in [latex]H[/latex] has an inverse, but [latex]H[/latex] is NOT a group.
For every [latex]A \in 2^X[/latex], the inverse of [latex]A[/latex] is the complement of [latex]A[/latex].
For every [latex]A \in 2^X[/latex], the inverse of [latex]A[/latex] is [latex]A[/latex].

questions.text:
Let [latex] f:A\rightarrow B[/latex] be an onto (or surjective) function, where [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are nonempty sets. Define an equivalence relation [latex] \sim [/latex] on the set [latex]A[/latex] as
[latex] a_1\sim a_2 \text{ if } f(a_1)=f(a_2),[/latex]
where [latex] a_1, a_2 \in A[/latex] . Let [latex] \varepsilon =\{[x]:x \in A\}[/latex] be the set of all the equivalence classes under [latex] \sim [/latex]. Define a new mapping [latex] F: \varepsilon \rightarrow B[/latex] as
[latex]F([x]) = f(x),[/latex] for all the equivalence classes [latex][x][/latex] in [latex] \varepsilon[/latex]
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Check each property of F:
- Well-defined: if [x] = [y], then f(x) = f(y), so F gives the same value for every representative (option 1 FALSE).
- Onto: for any b in B, f is onto, so f(a) = b for some a, and F([a]) = b.
- One-to-one: F([x]) = F([y]) means f(x) = f(y), so [latex]x\sim y[/latex] and [x] = [y].
- Onto and one-to-one [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] bijective.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: F is an onto (or surjective) function.
F is a one-to-one (or injective) function.

questions.text:
Let U = {1, 2,...,n}, where n is a large positive integer greater than 1000. Let k be a positive integer less than n. Let A, B be subsets of U with |A| = |B| = k and [latex] A\cap B=\phi [/latex]. We say that a permutation of U separates A from B if one of the following is true.

- All members of A appear in the permutation before any of the members of B.
- All members of B appear in the permutation before any of the members of A.

How many permutations of U separate A from B?
questions.solution:
Count the permutations step by step:
- Choose the 2k positions that A [latex]\cup[/latex] B will occupy: [latex]\binom{n}{2k}[/latex]
- Arrange the other [latex]n-2k[/latex] elements in the rest: [latex](n-2k)![/latex]
- In the chosen positions, put all of A first and then B, or B first and then A: 2 ways
- Arrange A among its k places and B among its k places: [latex](k!)^2[/latex]

Total [latex]=2\binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!(k!)^2[/latex]

Answer: [latex]2\binom{n}{2k}(n-2k)!(k!)^2[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
